The disclosure relates to fabrication techniques and integrated circuit (IC) configurations. These techniques allow a gate contact to be created on, or very near, a gate positioned over an active region of a field-effect transistor (FET), while reducing the risk of electrical shorts between the gate contact and metal plugs located on the source/drain regions, as well as between the gate and source/drain contacts connected to those metal plugs.

In the structure, a gate is formed over a channel region of the FET and includes both a dielectric cap and dielectric sidewall spacers. Metal plugs are then formed on the source/drain regions of the FET, with each plug also having an added dielectric cap. The dielectric sidewall spacer is positioned between the gate and the metal plugs, and also between the gate dielectric cap and the added dielectric caps on the plugs. The gate dielectric cap, the dielectric sidewall spacer, and the additional dielectric caps are made from different materials chosen in advance so that they can be etched selectively. The disclosure describes methods and integrated circuit structures for forming a gate contact on or near an active region of a field effect transistor. In particular, the described techniques address the challenge of placing a gate contact in close proximity to source/drain contacts while reducing the risk of unintended electrical shorting between conductive features.

In the disclosed structure, a gate is formed over a channel region of the transistor. The gate includes a dielectric cap on its upper surface and dielectric sidewall spacers along its sidewalls. Source/drain regions are positioned adjacent to the channel region, and metal plugs are formed on these source/drain regions to provide electrical connection. Additional dielectric caps are formed over the metal plugs. The sidewall spacer separates the gate from the adjacent metal plugs and their dielectric caps, helping to maintain electrical isolation between the gate structure and the source/drain contact structures.

The materials used for the gate cap, sidewall spacer, and plug caps are selected so that they can be etched selectively relative to one another and relative to the surrounding dielectric materials. This selective etch behavior allows a gate contact opening to be formed even if the contact is somewhat misaligned. Because the metal plugs remain protected by their dielectric caps and by the spacer structure during etching, the misaligned contact opening does not expose the metal plugs. As a result, the subsequently formed gate contact can land on or near the active region without creating an electrical short to the source/drain metal plugs.

Overall, the disclosed methods provide a more robust process window for forming gate contacts in highly scaled integrated circuits. By using dielectric caps and spacers with appropriate etch selectivity, the structure tolerates contact misalignment while preserving isolation between the gate contact and nearby source/drain contacts.
outputs.L4:
The disclosure relates to the fabrication of field-effect transistor (FET) integrated-circuit structures in which gate contacts may be formed over, adjacent to, or otherwise near active device regions without causing electrical shorts to neighboring conductive features. In advanced semiconductor devices, continued scaling reduces the spacing between gate structures, source/drain regions, and contact features, making conventional contact alignment increasingly difficult. Even small lithographic overlay errors during formation of contact openings can expose unintended conductive materials, such as a gate electrode, a source/drain contact, or a source/drain metal plug, thereby creating leakage paths or direct shorts that degrade device performance and yield.

To address these issues, the disclosed structure employs a protective dielectric arrangement around the gate and source/drain contact features. A gate dielectric cap is provided over the gate electrode, and dielectric sidewall spacers are formed along the sidewalls of the gate structure. These dielectric features electrically isolate the gate electrode from subsequently formed contact openings and conductive fills. In addition, source/drain metal plugs are formed with dielectric caps or with materials that can be selectively etched relative to surrounding dielectrics and conductive materials. The source/drain metal plugs may be recessed and capped so that, even if a gate contact opening is misaligned toward a source/drain region, the opening does not expose or electrically connect to the source/drain metal plug.

In some implementations, the materials used for the gate cap, sidewall spacers, source/drain plug caps, interlayer dielectrics, and conductive plugs are selected to provide strong etch selectivity during patterning. This allows contact openings to be etched in a self-aligned or partially self-aligned manner. For example, an etch process used to form a gate contact opening may remove one dielectric material while stopping on another dielectric cap or spacer, thereby preserving electrical isolation between the gate contact and nearby source/drain structures. Similarly, a source/drain contact opening may be formed without unintentionally penetrating the gate cap or spacer structure.

The disclosed configuration is particularly useful where a gate contact is placed over an active region, partially overlaps an active region, or is positioned very close to source/drain contacts. By surrounding the gate electrode with protective dielectric material and by capping the source/drain metal plugs, the structure can tolerate contact-opening misalignment caused by lithography or etch variation. If the contact opening shifts laterally from its intended position, the dielectric cap and spacer system prevents the conductive fill from contacting the wrong feature. As a result, gate-to-source/drain shorts, source/drain-to-gate shorts, and unintended connections between contact plugs and metal plugs are reduced or avoided.

The fabrication method may include forming one or more gate structures over a semiconductor substrate, forming source/drain regions adjacent to the gate structures, forming dielectric spacers on the gate sidewalls, depositing or otherwise forming source/drain metal plugs in contact with the source/drain regions, recessing the metal plugs, and forming dielectric caps over the recessed plugs. A gate cap may also be formed over the gate electrode before or during these operations. An interlayer dielectric may then be deposited over the device, followed by patterning and etching of contact openings for gate contacts and source/drain contacts. Because of the dielectric caps and spacers, the contact openings can be formed with relaxed overlay constraints. Conductive material is then deposited into the openings to form the final contacts.

This approach improves reliability by reducing the probability of electrical shorts and leakage paths in densely packed transistor layouts. It also supports continued device scaling by allowing contacts to be placed closer to one another and, in some cases, directly over or near active regions that would otherwise be excluded by conservative design rules. The use of selectively etchable materials further increases process margin, enabling more robust contact formation even in the presence of lithographic misalignment or etch nonuniformity. Consequently, the disclosed structures and methods provide greater layout flexibility, improved manufacturing yield, and enhanced scalability for advanced FET integrated circuits.

**Disclosed: The FET**

Disclosed here is a brief overview of the FET, or Field-Effect Transistor, an important electronic component used in countless modern devices. The FET controls the flow of electrical current through a semiconductor channel by applying voltage to a gate terminal. This makes it useful for switching, amplification, and signal control in circuits.

The main advantage of the FET is its high input impedance, which means it requires very little input current to operate. Because of this, FETs are widely used in computers, mobile phones, audio equipment, power supplies, and communication systems. Common types include the JFET and the MOSFET, with the MOSFET being especially important in digital electronics.

The FET has helped make electronic devices smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient. From simple circuits to advanced microprocessors, this component plays a key role in modern technology.

counterfactuals.output:
A semiconductor fabrication method can enable a gate contact to be placed over or very near an active device region while reducing the risk that a misaligned contact opening will short to source/drain contacts.

In one example flow:

1. **Form transistor structures**
   - A semiconductor substrate is patterned to define active regions, such as fins or planar active areas.
   - Gate structures are formed crossing the active regions.
   - Source/drain regions are formed adjacent to the gates, for example by epitaxial growth and/or implantation.

2. **Form source/drain contacts**
   - An interlayer dielectric is deposited over the device.
   - Contact openings are etched to the source/drain regions.
   - Conductive material, such as tungsten, cobalt, ruthenium, or another metal, is deposited to form source/drain contacts.

3. **Protect the source/drain contacts**
   - The source/drain contacts are recessed or otherwise covered.
   - A protective insulating cap or etch-stop layer is formed over the source/drain contacts.
   - This cap may be made from a material having etch selectivity relative to surrounding dielectrics, such as silicon nitride, silicon carbide, silicon carbon nitride, or another dielectric.

4. **Prepare the gate contact region**
   - A dielectric layer is deposited over the gate and source/drain contact level.
   - A gate contact opening is patterned. The opening may be intentionally located over the gate and may partially overlap the active region or be positioned close to source/drain contacts.

5. **Etch the gate contact opening with self-alignment protection**
   - During etching, the protective caps over the source/drain contacts act as barriers.
   - If the gate contact opening is misaligned and partially overlaps a source/drain contact, the cap prevents the etch from exposing the source/drain metal.
   - The etch selectively exposes the gate electrode or a gate contact landing region while leaving the protected source/drain contacts insulated.

6. **Fill the gate contact**
   - A conductive material is deposited into the gate contact opening.
   - Excess material is removed by planarization, forming a gate contact electrically connected to the gate electrode.

The key feature is the use of **protective dielectric caps or etch-stop structures over source/drain contacts**, allowing the gate contact opening to be patterned with relaxed alignment tolerance. Even if the gate contact opening is shifted toward a source/drain contact, the cap prevents accidental exposure and electrical shorting. This makes it possible to form a **gate contact over an active region or near source/drain contacts** while maintaining device reliability and enabling tighter layout scaling.

## Technical Disclosure: FET Gate Structures with Selectively Etchable Dielectric Caps, Sidewall Spacers, and Capped Source/Drain Metal Plugs

Disclosed are field-effect transistor (FET) structures and fabrication techniques in which gate structures and source/drain contact plugs include selectively etchable cap materials to improve patterning margin, reduce contact-to-gate shorts, and enable self-aligned contact integration.

In one embodiment, a semiconductor device includes a substrate having an active region and a gate stack disposed over a channel region of the active region. The gate stack may include a gate dielectric, a work-function metal and/or conductive gate electrode, and a dielectric gate cap formed on an upper surface of the gate electrode. The dielectric gate cap is formed from a material selectively etchable relative to adjacent interlayer dielectric material, sidewall spacer material, and/or source/drain plug cap material. Example gate cap materials include silicon nitride, silicon carbon nitride, silicon oxycarbonitride, aluminum oxide, hafnium oxide, or combinations thereof.

Sidewall spacers are disposed along opposing sidewalls of the gate stack. The spacers may include one or more dielectric layers, such as silicon nitride, silicon oxide, silicon carbide, silicon carbonitride, or low-k dielectric materials. In some embodiments, the spacer material is selected to exhibit etch selectivity relative to the gate cap and relative to a cap disposed over a source/drain metal plug. The sidewall spacers electrically isolate the gate electrode from adjacent source/drain contacts and define a self-aligned contact opening.

Raised or embedded source/drain regions are formed adjacent the gate structure. A conductive source/drain contact plug is disposed over each source/drain region and may include tungsten, cobalt, ruthenium, molybdenum, copper, titanium nitride, tantalum nitride, or another conductive material. A plug cap is formed on an upper surface of the source/drain metal plug. The plug cap comprises a dielectric, semiconductor, or metal-containing material that is selectively etchable relative to at least one of the interlayer dielectric, the gate cap, or the spacer material. Example plug cap materials include silicon nitride, silicon carbide, silicon carbonitride, aluminum oxide, titanium nitride, tantalum nitride, or ruthenium oxide, depending on the selected etch chemistry.

In certain implementations, the gate cap and source/drain plug cap are formed from different materials having mutually selective etch behavior. For example, the gate cap may be silicon nitride while the source/drain plug cap may be aluminum oxide, silicon carbide, or a metal nitride. This allows one cap to be recessed, removed, or opened without substantially attacking the other. In other implementations, the gate cap, spacer, and plug cap are each composed of different materials selected to provide three-way etch selectivity during formation of gate contacts, source/drain contacts, or local interconnects.

A representative fabrication method includes forming a gate stack over a semiconductor substrate, forming a dielectric gate cap over the gate electrode, and forming sidewall spacers along the gate stack. Source/drain regions are then formed adjacent the gate stack. An interlayer dielectric is deposited and patterned to form openings to the source/drain regions. A conductive metal is deposited in the openings to form source/drain plugs, followed by recessing the metal and depositing a plug cap over the recessed metal. Chemical mechanical planarization may be used to expose or level the gate cap, spacer, plug cap, and interlayer dielectric surfaces.

Subsequent contact or interconnect formation may use selective etch processes to remove one cap material while preserving another. For example, a source/drain contact opening may be etched through an interlayer dielectric and selectively stop on or remove the plug cap without eroding the gate cap or sidewall spacers. Conversely, a gate contact opening may selectively remove the gate cap while leaving capped source/drain plugs protected. The capped plug structure can thereby prevent inadvertent exposure of the source/drain metal during gate contact etching, while the capped gate structure prevents gate-to-contact shorting during source/drain contact patterning.

The disclosed structures are applicable to planar FETs, FinFETs, gate-all-around transistors, nanosheet transistors, nanowire transistors, forksheet devices, complementary FET structures, and other advanced transistor architectures. The selectively etchable cap scheme provides improved overlay tolerance, enhanced self-alignment capability, reduced parasitic leakage, and increased process robustness for dense transistor layouts.

counterfactuals.output:
Below is patent-style disclosure language describing methods and integrated circuit structures using different selectively etchable dielectric caps and spacers to provide contact misalignment tolerance in field-effect transistor devices.

---

## Technical Field

Embodiments described herein relate generally to semiconductor devices and methods of forming semiconductor devices, and more particularly to field-effect transistor structures including selectively etchable dielectric caps and spacer structures configured to provide increased tolerance to contact misalignment.

## Background

As semiconductor devices scale, alignment tolerances for source/drain contacts, gate contacts, and local interconnects become increasingly restrictive. Misalignment of a contact opening may result in unintended exposure of a gate electrode, source/drain region, epitaxial region, isolation structure, or adjacent conductive feature, thereby causing leakage, shorting, increased resistance, or device failure.

Self-aligned contact schemes may employ dielectric gate caps and sidewall spacers to protect gate electrodes during contact etching. However, conventional schemes using similar dielectric materials for caps and spacers may limit etch selectivity, reduce process margin, or require complex patterning. Accordingly, improved integrated circuit structures and fabrication methods are desirable in which different dielectric materials having different etch responses are strategically positioned to enable selective removal of one dielectric feature while retaining another dielectric feature, thereby increasing contact misalignment tolerance.

## Summary

In some embodiments, an integrated circuit structure includes a field-effect transistor having a gate structure disposed over a semiconductor body, a first dielectric cap disposed over the gate structure, a first dielectric spacer disposed along a sidewall of the gate structure, and a second dielectric spacer disposed laterally outward of the first dielectric spacer. The first dielectric cap, the first dielectric spacer, and the second dielectric spacer comprise different dielectric materials, or at least two of the dielectric materials are selectively etchable relative to one another. A source/drain contact is disposed adjacent to the gate structure and may at least partially overlap the first dielectric cap or one of the dielectric spacers in plan view without electrically shorting to the gate electrode.

In some embodiments, a method includes forming a gate structure over a semiconductor region, forming a first dielectric cap over the gate structure, forming a first dielectric spacer adjacent to the gate structure, forming a second dielectric spacer adjacent to the first dielectric spacer, forming a dielectric fill material over the source/drain region, and etching a contact opening through the dielectric fill material using an etch chemistry that selectively removes the dielectric fill material relative to the first dielectric cap and at least one of the first or second dielectric spacers. The contact opening may be laterally misaligned with respect to the source/drain region, and the selectively retained cap and spacer materials prevent exposure of the gate electrode.

In further embodiments, different selectively etchable dielectric caps and spacers are used to define multi-level etch-stop structures. For example, a gate cap may comprise silicon nitride, a first spacer may comprise silicon carbon nitride, and a second spacer may comprise silicon oxide, silicon oxycarbonitride, aluminum oxide, hafnium oxide, or another dielectric having a different etch rate in a selected contact etch chemistry. The different etch responses permit sequential or selective etching of contact openings while preserving selected protective dielectric elements.

---

## Detailed Description

### Device Structure

An integrated circuit structure may include a semiconductor substrate or semiconductor body. The semiconductor body may include silicon, silicon germanium, germanium, a III-V semiconductor material, a semiconductor-on-insulator structure, nanosheet channel structures, nanowire channel structures, fin structures, or any other suitable transistor channel material or architecture.

A field-effect transistor device is disposed over or within the semiconductor body. The field-effect transistor device may include:

1. a channel region;
2. a gate dielectric disposed adjacent to the channel region;
3. a gate electrode disposed over the gate dielectric;
4. source/drain regions disposed on opposing sides of the channel region; and
5. one or more dielectric caps and spacers disposed adjacent to the gate electrode.

The gate electrode may include one or more conductive materials, including but not limited to titanium nitride, tantalum nitride, tungsten, cobalt, ruthenium, molybdenum, aluminum, doped polysilicon, work-function metals, barrier metals, or combinations thereof. The gate dielectric may include silicon oxide, silicon oxynitride, hafnium oxide, zirconium oxide, aluminum oxide, lanthanum oxide, or another high-k dielectric material.

A first dielectric cap is disposed above the gate electrode. The first dielectric cap may function as a gate-protective cap during formation of a source/drain contact. In some embodiments, the first dielectric cap directly contacts an upper surface of the gate electrode. In other embodiments, one or more intervening dielectric or conductive layers are disposed between the gate electrode and the first dielectric cap.

A first sidewall spacer is disposed along a sidewall of the gate structure. The first sidewall spacer may directly contact the gate dielectric, the gate electrode, the first dielectric cap, or a liner layer adjacent thereto. A second sidewall spacer may be disposed laterally outward of the first sidewall spacer. Additional spacer layers may also be provided.

The first dielectric cap and the first and second sidewall spacers are selected so that at least one of the dielectric features is selectively etchable relative to another one of the dielectric features. In this manner, a contact etch may remove a dielectric fill or one spacer material while leaving another spacer material and/or gate cap substantially intact.

### Selectively Etchable Dielectric Materials

In various embodiments, the dielectric cap and spacer materials may be selected from materials including, but not limited to:

- silicon nitride;
- silicon carbon nitride;
- silicon boron carbon nitride;
- silicon oxycarbonitride;
- silicon oxide;
- carbon-doped silicon oxide;
- silicon oxynitride;
- aluminum oxide;
- aluminum nitride;
- hafnium oxide;
- zirconium oxide;
- titanium oxide;
- tantalum oxide;
- low-k dielectric materials;
- porous dielectric materials;
- air-gap-forming sacrificial materials; and
- combinations or multilayers thereof.

In one embodiment, the first dielectric cap comprises silicon nitride, the first spacer comprises silicon carbon nitride, and the second spacer comprises silicon oxide or silicon oxycarbonitride. In another embodiment, the first dielectric cap comprises aluminum oxide, the first spacer comprises silicon nitride, and the second spacer comprises silicon oxide. In yet another embodiment, the first dielectric cap comprises silicon carbon nitride, the first spacer comprises aluminum oxide, and the second spacer comprises silicon oxycarbonitride.

The phrase “selectively etchable” means that, under a given etch condition, one dielectric material is removed at a rate greater than another dielectric material. In some embodiments, the etch selectivity is at least about 2:1, at least about 5:1, at least about 10:1, or at least about 20:1. The etch may be a dry plasma etch, wet chemical etch, atomic layer etch, vapor phase etch, or combinations thereof.

By using different dielectric materials for caps and spacers, the contact opening may be etched even when the lithographic opening overlaps the gate region in plan view. The gate cap and one or more spacers remain as protective dielectric barriers, thereby preventing the contact from electrically contacting the gate electrode.

### Misalignment-Tolerant Source/Drain Contact

A dielectric layer, such as an interlayer dielectric, is disposed over the field-effect transistor. The dielectric layer may include silicon oxide, a low-k dielectric, flowable oxide, spin-on dielectric, carbon-doped oxide, or another insulating material.

A contact opening is formed through the dielectric layer to expose at least a portion of a source/drain region or a source/drain metallization feature. The contact opening may be laterally offset from an intended position. For example, the contact opening may overlap an upper surface of the gate cap, overlap a portion of a sidewall spacer, or extend partially over a region between adjacent transistors.

Because the gate cap and spacers are composed of selectively etch-resistant materials relative to the dielectric layer being etched, the contact etch does not substantially remove the protective cap and spacer features. The resulting contact may therefore be self-aligned to the gate structure despite lithographic misalignment.

A conductive contact material is then deposited in the contact opening. The conductive contact material may include tungsten, cobalt, ruthenium, molybdenum, copper, titanium, titanium nitride, tantalum, tantalum nitride, nickel, platinum, silicide, germanide, or combinations thereof. In some embodiments, a metal silicide or metal germanide is formed at the source/drain region prior to or during contact formation.

The contact may physically contact a source/drain region or a source/drain contact landing pad, while being laterally adjacent to and electrically isolated from the gate electrode by the retained dielectric cap and spacer structures.

### Example Method

In one embodiment, a method of forming an integrated circuit structure includes the following operations.

A semiconductor body is provided. The semiconductor body may include a fin, nanosheet stack, nanowire stack, planar semiconductor region, or other channel structure.

A gate structure is formed over the semiconductor body. The gate structure may be a sacrificial gate structure used in a replacement metal gate process, or may be a final gate structure. In a replacement metal gate embodiment, a sacrificial gate is formed, source/drain regions are formed, the sacrificial gate is removed, and a final gate dielectric and metal gate electrode are formed in the resulting gate trench.

A first dielectric cap is formed over the gate structure. The first dielectric cap comprises a first dielectric material. The first dielectric material may be selected to resist a subsequent contact etch. In some embodiments, the first dielectric cap is recessed relative to an interlayer dielectric and then formed by depositing dielectric material over the gate electrode and planarizing the dielectric material.

A first spacer is formed along sidewalls of the gate structure. The first spacer comprises a second dielectric material different from the first dielectric material. The first spacer may be formed by conformal deposition followed by anisotropic etching.

A second spacer is formed along sidewalls of the first spacer. The second spacer comprises a third dielectric material different from the first and second dielectric materials. In some embodiments, the second spacer is selectively removable relative to the first spacer and the first dielectric cap. In other embodiments, the second spacer is more etch resistant than an adjacent interlayer dielectric and functions as an additional contact etch stop.

Source/drain regions are formed adjacent to the gate structure. The source/drain regions may include epitaxial semiconductor material such as silicon, silicon germanium, silicon carbide, germanium, or III-V semiconductor material. Dopants may be introduced in situ during epitaxial growth or by implantation.

An interlayer dielectric is deposited over the source/drain regions and the gate structure. The interlayer dielectric may be planarized.

A contact opening is patterned over a source/drain region. The contact opening may be wider than the source/drain region or may be intentionally permitted to overlap the gate cap or spacer in plan view.

The contact opening is etched using a first etch chemistry that removes the interlayer dielectric selectively relative to the first dielectric cap and at least one spacer. Where the contact opening overlaps the gate structure, the first dielectric cap prevents exposure of the gate electrode. Where the contact opening overlaps a gate sidewall region, one or more spacers prevent lateral exposure of the gate electrode.

In some embodiments, a second etch chemistry is used to selectively remove a portion of one spacer or a liner while preserving the gate cap. This may enlarge the contact landing area or expose a source/drain surface without exposing the gate electrode.

A conductive material is deposited in the contact opening to form a source/drain contact. A planarization process may remove excess conductive material above the interlayer dielectric.

The resulting contact may be misaligned relative to the source/drain region by an amount that would otherwise expose or short to the gate electrode in a conventional structure. The selectively etchable cap and spacer system provides a dielectric shield and thereby increases overlay tolerance.

### Sequential Selective Etch Embodiments

In some embodiments, the use of different cap and spacer materials permits a sequential etching process.

For example, an interlayer dielectric comprising silicon oxide is etched using a fluorocarbon plasma that etches silicon oxide faster than silicon nitride or silicon carbon nitride. The etch stops on or slows upon reaching a silicon nitride gate cap and a silicon carbon nitride inner spacer.

A second etch may then selectively remove a silicon oxycarbonitride outer spacer or liner relative to the silicon nitride gate cap. This may expose a source/drain contact area while preserving gate protection.

A third surface preparation or breakthrough etch may remove native oxide from the source/drain region while having low etch rate to the retained cap and spacer materials.

This sequence allows a contact opening to be formed with a relaxed lithographic overlay requirement because the contact profile is defined at least in part by material selectivity rather than solely by lithographic placement.

### Integrated Circuit Structure Embodiments

In some embodiments, an integrated circuit structure comprises:

- a semiconductor body;
- a gate structure over the semiconductor body, the gate structure including a gate electrode;
- a gate cap over the gate electrode, the gate cap comprising a first dielectric material;
- an inner spacer on a sidewall of the gate structure, the inner spacer comprising a second dielectric material selectively etchable relative to the first dielectric material;
- an outer spacer laterally adjacent to the inner spacer, the outer spacer comprising a third dielectric material selectively etchable relative to at least one of the first dielectric material and the second dielectric material;
- a source/drain region adjacent to the gate structure;
- an interlayer dielectric over the source/drain region; and
- a conductive contact extending through the interlayer dielectric to the source/drain region.

The conductive contact may have a sidewall that is laterally offset over the gate cap in plan view. The conductive contact may overlie a portion of the gate cap but may be electrically isolated from the gate electrode by the gate cap. The conductive contact may also contact or be bounded by one of the inner spacer or outer spacer.

In some embodiments, the gate cap has a first etch rate in a contact etch chemistry, the inner spacer has a second etch rate in the contact etch chemistry, and the outer spacer has a third etch rate in the contact etch chemistry. At least two of the first, second, and third etch rates differ by a factor of at least 5. In further embodiments, the interlayer dielectric has an etch rate greater than each of the gate cap and the inner spacer in the contact etch chemistry.

### Additional Embodiments

In some embodiments, the first dielectric cap is recessed below an upper surface of the interlayer dielectric and is laterally confined between spacer structures. In other embodiments, the first dielectric cap extends laterally over at least a portion of a spacer. In still other embodiments, the gate cap includes multiple layers, such as a silicon nitride layer and an aluminum oxide layer, to provide etch resistance to multiple etch chemistries.

In some embodiments, the spacer system includes an inner low-k spacer to reduce parasitic capacitance and an outer etch-stop spacer to provide contact alignment tolerance. For example, the inner spacer may comprise silicon oxycarbonitride or carbon-doped oxide, and the outer spacer may comprise silicon nitride, silicon carbon nitride, or aluminum oxide.

In some embodiments, the selectively etchable dielectric features are used with fin field-effect transistors, gate-all-around transistors, nanosheet transistors, complementary FET structures, forksheet transistors, vertical FETs, or planar FETs.

In some embodiments, a gate contact may also be formed using selective etching. A second cap material may be disposed over source/drain contacts or source/drain regions, and a gate contact opening may be etched selectively relative to such second cap material. Thus, different dielectric caps may independently protect gate features and source/drain features during formation of different contact levels.
